source.title: Batch Normalization Alleviates the Spectral Bias in Coordinate Networks
source.authors: Zhicheng Cai; Hao Zhu; Qiu Shen; Xin-Ran Wang; Xun Cao

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no material cutoff is apparent. The title in the header differs slightly from the catalog title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments and theoretical analyses on how normalization affects coordinate-network training dynamics and signal reconstruction, a related but different setting from the claim’s classification-error benchmarks.
record.gate_note: No results directly measure training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, training with corrupted or random labels, bad local minima, residual shortcuts, or training above a stability threshold. Results on reconstruction quality, spectral components, and convergence are relevant to normalization and initialization versions. The paper cites prior normalization work but those cited results are not extracted as this paper’s own findings.
record.test_reason: The study reports faster training with BN in a new setting: ReLU coordinate networks fitting signals and images. This bears on V6's training-speed component. It does not compare initialization schemes, so it does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue theoretically that BN and LN improve coordinate-network NTK eigenvalue distributions, empirically report spectral-bias alleviation and faster high-frequency convergence with all four normalizations, and report improved reconstruction performance, with CN often strongest.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies coordinate networks on signal representation and inverse reconstruction tasks, using NTK analysis and normalization comparisons; the claim versions focus on classification benchmarks, depth/shortcuts, initialization, learning-rate stability, and specific BN settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization type and task differ in reported outcomes; CN is often strongest, and the study uses different initial learning rates for normalized versus unnormalized image-compression methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalization shifts the NTK eigenvalue distribution and reduces its largest eigenvalues.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization changes coordinate-network NTK spectra in ways associated with reduced spectral bias.

fits_no_version.finding: LN, global normalization and cross normalization accelerate frequency learning and image fitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization methods beyond BN can accelerate coordinate-network training.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized coordinate networks improve final shape, CT and MRI reconstruction metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization improves coordinate-network reconstruction quality under the tested training budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: CN improves average MipNeRF PSNR from 33.58 to 33.91 and NeuS chamfer distance from 0.80 to 0.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross normalization can improve final neural rendering and surface-reconstruction quality.

record.problems: The experiments focus on coordinate-network signal reconstruction rather than classification error. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The image-compression convergence comparison uses different initial learning rates for normalized and unnormalized methods. Some table content, notably Table 7, is flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Table 4 reports additional normalization and positional-encoding variants; only the explicitly discussed ReLU+BN result was retained to keep extraction focused. Table 7 values are not reconstructed from the flattened table.

untested.parts: CIFAR training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and model-size, early-stopping and regularization conditions.
Teacher-student ReLU spurious minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth degradation, identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh training and normalization-free residual training.
All initialization comparisons and trainable-depth claims. Using specified initialization schemes without varying them does not test their effects.
Stability thresholds, loss recovery, divergence and curvature or sharpness trajectories.

The original classification settings, controlled learning-rate-tolerance comparisons, matched-learning-rate image-training comparisons, and Fixup residual networks. Successful training at a larger selected learning rate does not establish that the unnormalized network cannot tolerate it.

missing.what: Fig. 3 also includes the PEMLP-5 versus PEMLP-5+BN frequency-specific training comparison. Add a separate row describing what those curves show; R3 covers only PEMLP-1.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text explicitly identifies itself as an expanded version of the CVPR 2024 paper, with new LN/GN/CN analyses and reconducted experiments. Those expanded results should not be attributed without qualification to the conference DOI. Different tasks and untested claim components are not grounds for a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size and early stopping effects.
Teacher-student ReLU minima and extra student width.
Plain versus residual shortcut depth effects; normalization-free residual training.

Activation-matched initialization comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and very deep plain networks. Experiments use coordinate networks and their stated initialization schemes, not the version’s depth and initialization comparisons.
Learning-rate stability threshold, loss rise and recovery, curvature and sharpness trajectories.
The listed sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10 and Inception ImageNet settings, higher-learning-rate tolerance comparisons, and Fixup residual networks are not tested.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared NTK eigenvalue distributions for ReLU coordinate networks with and without normalization.
rows.measure: NTK eigenvalue distribution; histogram peak and largest eigenvalue
rows.baseline: without normalization: peak probability ∼10−3; largest eigenvalues ∼106
rows.value: with BN, LN, GN, CN: peak probability ∼100, 10−1, ∼10−2, ∼100.1 respectively; largest eigenvalues reduced to ∼105
rows.note: The paper describes the distribution as shifting from lower to higher values; it does not report classification error.
rows.check: NTK spectra under different normalizations do not measure initialization-dependent speed or trainable depth, or directly establish faster training. The reported powers of ten locate histogram peaks on the eigenvalue axis; they are not peak probabilities.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.stage_stated: trained for iterations; optimizer not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency-specific approximation error over training iterations.
rows.baseline: without normalization, high-frequency error reduces slowly; exact value not stated
rows.value: with normalization, especially CN, error reduces to < 0.2 and converges at a very early stage
rows.note: Described as frequency-specific training error, not classification error.
rows.check: Relink from V4 to V6 for the BN versus unnormalized comparison. Split BN from LN, GN and CN, which V6 does not name. Section 4.4.2 reports faster high-frequency convergence with normalization; the pooled error below 0.2 should not be assigned separately to every method without reading its curve.

source_check.problem: Matches the supplied extension's collective normalization result; neither CVPR provenance nor a BN-specific below-0.2 value is verified.

rows.subject: PEMLP
rows.stage_stated: trained for iterations; optimizer not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency-specific approximation error over training iterations.
rows.value: with normalization, especially CN, error reduces to < 0.2 and converges at a very early stage
rows.note: The paper calls this a frequency-specific training error.
rows.check: Relink from V4 to V6 for the BN comparison and split other normalization types into separate rows with versions ['none']. The approximately 0.4 baseline and below-0.2 normalized error are described collectively for PE and normalization, rather than established separately for each extracted condition.

source_check.locator_found: Supplied extension, Section 4.4.2, lines 1289–1299; Fig. 3 panels f–j.
source_check.problem: The approximately 0.4 baseline and below-0.2 normalized error are collective prose claims, not individually stated PEMLP-1/BN cells; CVPR provenance is unverified.

rows.subject: ReLU coordinate networks
rows.operation_detail: Added BN, LN, GN, or CN before ReLU activations and compared image reconstruction training curves and PSNR.

conditions.value: normalized methods use initial 1e−2; other methods use 2e−4

rows.measure: Training PSNR convergence speed and reconstruction PSNR
rows.baseline: ReLU without normalization; table reports [13×49] PSNR 24.33
rows.value: For [13×49], ReLU+BN 29.08, ReLU+LN 28.26, ReLU+GN 27.86, ReLU+CN 29.22; text says normalizations accelerate convergence and significantly enhance PSNR
rows.note: Reconstruction task, not classification accuracy. The differing initial learning rates mean the speed comparison is not an isolated normalization-only comparison.
rows.check: Retain the BN training-curve comparison for V6; split LN, GN and CN into separate rows with versions ['none']. Fig. 4c supplies the speed evidence; final Table 2 PSNR alone does not. Normalized networks use learning rate 0.01 versus 0.0002, so the comparison concerns the reported recipes and does not isolate BN at a matched learning rate.

rows.subject: ReLU coordinate networks
rows.operation_detail: Added BN, LN, GN, or CN to ReLU coordinate networks and compared shape reconstruction IoU.
rows.note: Reconstruction representation quality, not a direct training-speed or classification-error measure.
rows.check: Final shape-representation IoU after 200 epochs does not establish faster training or greater learning-rate tolerance.

rows.subject: PE coordinate networks
rows.operation_detail: Added BN, LN, GN, or CN to positional-encoding ReLU coordinate networks and compared shape reconstruction IoU.
rows.note: The paper reports improvements averaged across eight shapes; this metric does not directly assess classification training error or convergence speed.
rows.check: Final IoU improvement does not measure V6's training-speed effect. Its small magnitude is not evidence that V6 holds partially.

rows.subject: ReLU coordinate networks
rows.operation_detail: Added BN, LN, GN, or CN to ReLU coordinate networks and compared CT reconstruction quality.
rows.value: ReLU+BN [2×128] PSNR 28.50, SSIM 0.882; text also reports ReLU+BN competitive against existing methods
rows.note: This row records the BN result described in the text; other normalization table entries are not separately narrated and omitted for concision.
rows.check: Reconstruction PSNR and SSIM do not measure training speed or learning-rate tolerance. The extracted numerical comparison is specifically ReLU+BN at [2×128]; its condition should not encompass every normalization and architecture. Table 4 includes [4×256], although the configuration paragraph lists only three architectures.

rows.subject: ReLU coordinate networks
rows.operation_detail: Added BN, LN, GN, or CN to ReLU coordinate networks and compared MRI reconstruction PSNR.
rows.note: Authors state normalizations considerably improve ReLU performance; reconstructed PSNR is not classification error.
rows.check: Final MRI reconstruction quality after a fixed iteration budget does not establish convergence speed or learning-rate tolerance. The numerical values shown apply specifically to [4×256].

rows.subject: MipNeRF with CN
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross normalization to MipNeRF and compared novel-view-synthesis results with the original MipNeRF.
rows.note: The improvement is small and reported on a view-synthesis task. The paper says average PSNR improves up to 0.33dB.
rows.check: CN is not BN, and novel-view reconstruction quality does not measure V6's training-speed effect. MipNeRF is an application model rather than a toy network.

rows.subject: NeuS with CN
rows.operation_detail: Applied cross normalization to NeuS and compared reconstruction chamfer distance with the original NeuS.
rows.baseline: NeuS average value not recoverable from flattened table
rows.value: Ours average value not recoverable from flattened table; text states average chamfer distance improves up to 6.25%
rows.note: The table text is flattened and does not preserve average-column assignments reliably; the paper explicitly states the aggregate improvement.
rows.check: CN-enhanced NeuS reconstruction quality does not measure any supplied version. Table 7's continuation permits recovery of the average chamfer distances: NeuS 0.80 and Ours 0.75, matching the stated 6.25% reduction. NeuS is an application model rather than a toy network.

relationships.reason: R2–R5 and Sections 4.4.2 and 5.1 report faster convergence with BN; the image results compare recipes using 0.01 with normalization versus 0.0002 without it, so they do not isolate a matched-rate BN effect.
relationships.display_finding: Batch normalization accelerated convergence, but image comparisons used learning rates of 0.01 with normalization versus 0.0002 without it.
